title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Problem II of E740 asks for a space curve (x, y(x), z(x)) that makes J = ∫ (y+z) y' z' dx stationary. With p = y' and q = z', the Lagrangian is V = pq(y+z). On the previous page Euler writes the Euler–Lagrange system. One equation is the energy (Beltrami) first integral, S = V − Pp − P'q = −pq(y+z) = const. The other two are pq = d/dx[(y+z)q] and pq = d/dx[(y+z)p]. From these he gets y+z = a/(pq), then dp/p² = dq/q², hence q = cp/(c+p), y+z = a(c+p)/(cp²), dx = −a(c+p)dp/(cp⁴) and x = a/(3p³) + a/(2cp²) + f.

This page:
(§17) From dy = p dx he gets dy = −a(c+p)dp/(cp³), hence y = a/(2p²) + a/(cp) + g. The algebraic relation for y+z then gives z = a/(2p²) − g. There are four arbitrary constants a, c, f, g, so Euler declares the solution complete.

(§18) Points of the curve are obtained by giving values to the parameter p. Euler argues the curve is not plane because no relation αx+βy+γz=0 can be formed. To eliminate p he uses y−z = a/(cp) + 2g, so p = a/(c(y−z−2g)). Substituting into z+g = a/(2p²) gives 2a(z+g) = c²(y−z−2g)², a parabolic cylinder over the (y,z)-plane. Substituting into the x-formula gives a second surface. He remarks these implicit equations are useless for drawing the curve, and that the curve is algebraic, unlike the extremal of Problem I.

Modern reading: put t = 1/p. Then
- x = (a/3)t³ + (a/2c)t² + f,
- y = (a/2)t² + (a/c)t + g,
- z = (a/2)t² − g.
This is a polynomial cubic parametrization with 1, t, t², t³ independent, i.e. a twisted cubic: a non-planar, rational normal curve of degree 3. Since V is quadratic in the velocities and x plays the role of time, the extremals are affinely parametrized geodesics of the indefinite metric (y+z) dy dz. In u = y+z, v = y−z this is (u/4)(du² − dv²). Translation in v is a symmetry, giving the constant g; translation in x gives f. The (y,z)-projections of these geodesics are the parabolas above.
errors: Planarity criterion stated as αx+βy+γz=0 without a constant term. It should be αx+βy+γz=δ, since the constants f and g shift the origin. The conclusion remains true because 1, t, t², t³ are linearly independent.
Completeness is asserted only by counting four constants. Degenerate cases are not discussed: a=0 (p=0, q=0, or y+z=0) and the division steps by p, q, p².
No computational errors: x, y, z all check, dz = q dx is consistent, and the elimination 2a(z+g) = c²(y−z−2g)² is correct.

ideas.what: Integration of the Euler–Lagrange system for ∫(y+z)y'z'dx in parametric form, using the energy first integral and the parameter p = y'
ideas.modern_name: Beltrami identity / energy integral; parametric solution of Euler–Lagrange equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744) and Lagrange; energy integral in mechanics
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65) for the plane case; this paper E740 for three coordinates

ideas.what: The extremal is a non-planar algebraic curve given by a cubic polynomial parametrization (a twisted cubic)
ideas.modern_name: twisted cubic / rational normal curve of degree 3
ideas.usually_credited_to: Möbius and the 19th-century projective geometers (twisted cubics)
ideas.where_published: E740 (this page); Euler does not name the curve type

ideas.what: Planarity test by checking whether a linear relation among x, y, z exists after eliminating the parameter
ideas.modern_name: linear independence of coordinate functions / non-degeneracy of a space curve
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; Clairaut and Euler on curves of double curvature
ideas.where_published: Euler's treatment of space curves, e.g. Introductio vol. II appendix

missed.claim: Euler's algebraic extremal is in fact a twisted cubic: polynomial of degree 3 in t = 1/p. It is also an affinely parametrized geodesic of the Lorentzian metric (y+z) dy dz, whose (y,z)-projections are parabolas. Euler notes only that the curve is 'algebraic' and non-planar.
missed.quote: Caeterum evidens est hanc curvam esse algebraicam, secus atque ea quae problemate praecedente erat inventa.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is only a nice pedagogical example of a twisted cubic arising as a variational extremal. It is not a substantive gap in the literature.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example of Euler's three-coordinate variational method; the calculations are correct and standard. The only extra observation is that the extremal is a twisted cubic, which is easy and of minor interest.
transcription_corrections: 'haud difficultur' is as printed (a misprint in the original); the intended word is 'difficulter'.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image; 'introductae' and the fraction forms are correct.
